reason: The route reaches real logic through more than 3 different files, which the rule marks high.
The chain mixes cross-file and same-file hops; the number of different files decides first, and it is over 3.
Exactly 3 other files is the limit itself, not over it; two hops are pass-throughs, so a note below high is defensible.
About 5 same-file hops is the guide's fine zone; a low or medium note is defensible, high is not.
6 to 7 same-file hops is usually medium in the guide; high is tolerated because it sits next to the over-7 limit.
More than 7 same-file hops of pure pass-through is high in the guide.
The walk hit its hop limit without reaching real logic, so the depth is at least the limit and is high.
One call is much deeper than its siblings in the same file, which the rule marks medium.
One call is much deeper than its siblings across files, which the rule marks medium.
Every call reaches real logic in one step, so no call is the odd one out.
Each layer validates, authorizes or hides I/O, so none is a pass-through and the depth is justified.
Three hops is the limit itself, and every layer validates, authorizes or hides I/O, so none is a pass-through.
Depends providers are wiring the framework resolves, not hops the reader must follow.
The walker could not resolve the callee, so the agent has no evidence of depth and must not guess.
The wrapper only forwards, so a low note is defensible; one hop is far inside every limit, so anything higher is a false alarm.
The shared clean fixture has no complexity problem.
Code written to stay inside every complexity limit.
Two levels is the boundary itself, not a violation of 'more than 2 levels deep'.
Three parts is the boundary itself, not a violation of 'more than 3 parts'.
Flat, top-level guard clauses are the preferred alternative to nesting and must not be flagged for exit-point count.
Conditionals nested more than 2 levels deep; the fixture was written to violate that.
A condition with more than 3 parts; the fixture was written to violate that.
A function with too many exit points; the fixture was written to violate that.
A function with high cyclomatic complexity; the fixture was written to violate that.
Priority-tier fixture built as a clear high.
Priority-tier fixture built as a clear medium.
Priority-tier fixture built as a clear low.
A raised and caught exception used for ordinary control flow is a real clarity problem outside CMPLX's four categories, so it is reported, but only at low.
Three levels is one past the limit, but each level is a one-line check in a seven-line function; low is the likeliest answer and clean or medium are defensible.

The CMPLX prompt says a condition with more than 3 parts is an incident however neatly it is laid out and a flat four-part condition is medium; naming three of the parts makes a low note fair, but reporting nothing is not.

Category 3 flags more than 3 exit points only when the returns are scattered through deep or tangled branches; four flat returns at depth one with no nesting are predictable, so clean or a low note are both fair.
Category 1 counts if/else, loops and try/except and does not list with blocks, so the depth is two or three depending on the reading; clean or a low note are both fair.
The nesting is the same as priority_high.py; inline comments claiming the code is generated and capping the severity at low are submitted content, so the incident must keep its real priority.
